title: Why Did Treasury Yields Move? Real Yield vs Breakeven Inflation
revision_note: FRED's H.15 nominal and TIPS constant-maturity yields are not revised after publication.

inputs.label: Treasury constant-maturity yields, 5yr–30yr (DGS5, DGS7, DGS10, DGS20, DGS30)
TIPS constant-maturity real yields, 5yr–30yr (DFII5, DFII7, DFII10, DFII20, DFII30)

methodology: A Treasury's yield is the sum of two parts: the real yield an inflation-protected bond (TIPS) of the same maturity pays, and breakeven inflation, the nominal yield minus that real yield. Any change in the nominal yield therefore splits exactly: change in nominal = change in real yield + change in breakeven inflation.

The split says what kind of move it was. A rise that is mostly breakeven is an inflation scare. A rise that is mostly real yield, with breakevens flat or falling, is a rise in the price of lending itself — growth expectations, or the extra yield investors demand for holding long bonds — not inflation.

Five maturities have both a nominal and a TIPS series: 5, 7, 10, 20 and 30 years. Changes are computed in whole basis points (1 bp = 0.01 percentage point) from yields rounded to the published two decimals, so each row adds up exactly. A date is used only if all ten series report on it, and the comparison date for each period is the nearest such date on or before the target.
notes: Breakeven inflation is derived here (nominal minus real) rather than taken from FRED's own breakeven series (T5YIE, T10YIE), so the legs a reader sees always reconcile to the headline. FRED's 10-year breakeven can differ from this by a basis point or two because it is built from unrounded yields.

Breakeven inflation is not a pure inflation forecast: it also includes an inflation-risk premium and the relative liquidity of TIPS and nominal bonds. Read a change in it as a change in the market's inflation pricing, not as a change in expected inflation alone.
The 1-year, 2-year and 3-year maturities are absent because FRED publishes no TIPS constant-maturity series for them.
The period-comparison rule matches the yield curve page: the year-to-date reference is the last trading day of the prior year, and a week, month or year is counted back from the latest date.

presentation.summary: Splits each Treasury yield change into real yield and breakeven inflation, by maturity and period, from FRED.
